Neonates of the Ground pangolin weigh approximately 340 grams [Wwb = approximately 340 grams] at birth, a modest mass that is typical for myrmecophagous mammals and represents roughly two percent of the ultimate adult body mass. These newborns measure about 15 centimetres in length, though they remain entirely dependent on the mother for nourishment and transport during the initial weeks of life.

For the first several months, the nursing offspring clings to the maternal tail or base of the back, suckling regularly. Weaning from milk typically occurs around three months after parturition (3 months after birth) [tx = 3 months after birth], a developmental milestone reached when the young pangolin begins to consume termites and ants independently at a temperature of 33.4 °C [T = 33.4 °C]. This transition to solid food marks the onset of nutritional independence, though the juvenile may continue to associate with its mother for some time afterward.

Adult body mass in this species shows considerable variation, but the maximum weight recorded among males from available data reaches 16.1 kilograms [Wwi = 16.1 kilograms], an ultimate size that reflects the animal’s robust, heavily scaled build. Sub-adult individuals, defined as those weighing less than 8 kilograms [Wwp = 8 kilograms], are considered not yet fully mature and are often observed foraging alone without engaging in reproductive activities. The attainment of puberty, however, is not closely tied to this specific mass threshold. Field records suggest that both sexes may reach sexual maturity at approximately two years after birth [tp = approximately two years after birth], although they might roam and forage for several additional years before actually attempting to breed. This protracted period between reaching physical maturity and initiating reproduction is unusual among mammals of comparable size and may be linked to the challenges of establishing a home range in a landscape with patchy termite resources.

Gestation in the Ground pangolin lasts between 105 and 140 days (105-140 days) [tg = 105-140 days], a relatively short duration for a mammal of this adult mass. Females give birth to a single offspring per clutch [N_R_i = single offspring per clutch], though twins have been recorded occasionally, and there is evidence that females may become pregnant while still nursing their current young. Despite this potential for overlapping litters, the overall reproductive rate remains low: females possibly give birth only every second year, yielding approximately 0.5 litters per year [F_R_i = approximately 0.5 litters per year]. This low fecundity is offset by a notably long lifespan. Although hard data are scarce, authors estimate that individuals may live between 20 and 30 years, with a plausible maximum longevity of approximately 25 years [am = approximately 25 years]. The combination of a late age at first breeding, extended inter-birth intervals, and modest litter size renders the Ground pangolin highly vulnerable to population declines from even low levels of anthropogenic mortality.

During the nursing period, a female Ground pangolin maintains a relatively stable core body temperature of 33.4 °C [T = 33.4 °C] while actively foraging and carrying her dependent offspring. This relatively low thermoregulatory set point for a eutherian mammal likely reflects the species’ myrmecophagous diet and its energetic economy. The same thermal regime appears to be important for the developing offspring as well, with weaning onset occurring at roughly three months (roughly 3 months after birth) [tx = roughly 3 months after birth] under these conditions — a duration that is consistent with the prolonged maternal care observed in other African pangolins at a temperature of 33.4 °C [T = 33.4 °C]. The low daily energy expenditure associated with a 33.4 °C body temperature may also constrain the maximum reproductive rate, contributing to the observed pattern of single young and biennial breeding. In contrast to species with higher metabolic rates, the Ground pangolin cannot sustain the energetic demands of rapid serial reproduction, a constraint that reinforces its status as one of the slowest-living mammals in the African savanna.

The maximum reproductive output, when expressed as a daily rate, is calculated from one pup per litter every two years, reflecting an exceptionally slow life-history strategy even among myrmecophages. This prolonged inter-birth interval, combined with the modest litter size, underscores the species' vulnerability to anthropogenic pressures and highlights the importance of protecting adult females to sustain population viability.
